opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, there are a few channels, and they all matter in different ways. The most direct one is just using the models and paying attention to how they behave. When you see a response that feels off, whether it's too cautious, too preachy, or it missed what you actually wanted, that's really valuable signal. Thumbs-down feedback in the product, with a note about what went wrong, does make its way back to us. It helps us figure out whether the model is failing to follow the spec or whether the spec itself is asking for the wrong thing.

Second, we've published the Model Spec openly precisely so people can read it and push back on it. We want people to engage with the actual text: point to a specific principle or example and say, "I think this is the wrong call, and here's why," or "this is ambiguous, and here's a case where two sections seem to conflict." That kind of concrete, case-based feedback is by far the most useful, because the hard part of writing a spec isn't stating high-level values everyone agrees with. It's deciding what happens at the edges, when helpfulness, safety, and respect for the user's autonomy pull in different directions.

We've also done more structured things, like collecting public input and running studies where we ask people from different backgrounds how they think the model should behave in specific scenarios. That helps us see where our defaults might reflect our own blind spots rather than what people broadly want.

And finally, people write about it. Researchers, journalists, developers building on the platform, people posting on social media. We read a lot of that. Some of the most useful critiques have come from someone writing a thoughtful post about a behavior they found frustrating and tracing it back to a particular line in the spec.

If I had to boil it down, I'd say the best feedback is specific. Show us the prompt, show us the response, tell us what you expected and why. That gives us something we can actually act on, and it keeps the spec a living document rather than something we write once and forget about.

r001.rationale: The response describes public input, studies, and outside critiques as useful feedback, but does not state that many Model Spec changes have resulted from feedback submitted by members of the public.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the most useful feedback is specific and grounded in a concrete case. Telling us "the spec feels too restrictive" is hard to act on. Telling us "here's a prompt, here's what the model did, here's what the spec says it should do, and here's why I think those are in tension" is something we can actually take back to the table and argue about.

In terms of channels, the spec is published openly, and we've set up public comment periods where we solicit input directly, and we read what comes in. People also reach out through our research and policy teams, through our developer forums, and increasingly just by publishing critiques, blog posts, papers, threads, and we do pay attention to those. Some of the most pointed feedback we've gotten has come from people who sat down with the document and found internal contradictions, or found a principle that sounds good in the abstract but produces a weird outcome when you trace it through an example.

The thing I'd encourage is to engage with the spec as a document with a structure. There's the chain of command, the objectives, the rules, the defaults. If you think a default should be different, say which one and what you'd replace it with. If you think two rules conflict, show the case where they collide. And if you're a developer building on the API, tell us where the spec got in your way or where a behavior you observed didn't match what the spec says. That mismatch between the written spec and actual model behavior is some of the highest-signal feedback we get, because it tells us either the training isn't landing or the spec isn't saying what we meant.

And disagreement is welcome. The whole point of writing it down publicly is so people can push on it. It's meant to be a living document, and the revisions we've shipped have come substantially from outside input.

r001.rationale: The response says shipped revisions came “substantially from outside input” and describes public comments and critiques as feedback channels, conveying that public feedback has driven many changes.

astra-6.text:
I think the most useful feedback is concrete. If you read something in the Model Spec that you disagree with, give us an example of a situation where you think it would lead to the wrong behavior, and tell us what you’d want the model to do instead. That makes the tradeoff much easier to discuss.

And I’d distinguish between two kinds of feedback: “The model isn’t following the spec,” and “The model is following the spec, but I think the spec should be different.” Both are valuable. We want to understand where the behavior falls short, but also where people disagree with the behavior we’re aiming for.

r001.rationale: The response encourages concrete feedback and distinguishes types of feedback, but does not state that many Model Spec changes have resulted from feedback submitted by the public.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful feedback is concrete: “Here’s a situation, here’s what the model did, and here’s what I think it should have done instead.” That helps us distinguish between a model failing to follow the spec and a place where the spec itself should change.

It’s also valuable to point out tradeoffs. If you disagree with a principle, tell us why, who it affects, and what you’d propose instead. You don’t need to be an AI researcher to contribute—examples from your own experience can make those questions much clearer.

r001.rationale: The response recommends concrete feedback and proposals, but does not state that many Model Spec changes have come from feedback submitted by the public.
